newsitem.title: UK: British funds have no appetite for yen plays now.
newsitem.headline: British funds have no appetite for yen plays now.

text.p: British-based investment managers, having witnessed a dramatic yen appreciation in recent weeks, see little chance of further gains by the Japanese currency in the immediate term.
Many see the yen stabilising around current levels, but even if the yen calms down some saw opportunities for gains in Japanese stocks.

"The authorities are just trying to manage (yen) levels -- a lot of it is just jawboning," said David Heath, senior fund manager at Axa Equity & Law Investment Management, who has some 400 million stg in Japanese equities.
"There were comments at about 125 yen/dollar and now at 111 yen/dollar."

The dollar regained lost ground against the yen on Thursday -- rising some 4.5 yen at one point -- after influential Japanese official Eisuke Sakakibara said that an interest rate rise was not imminent and that fears of a ballooning trade surplus were overblown.

Fund managers, who in past weeks were scrutinising the Japanese economy for signs of a recovery that could lead to rising interest rates and a repatriation of yen assets, are now taking a more sober view.

"In order for us to be more bullish on the yen we would need an appreciable positive economic surprise that could be the start of an aggressive change of policy by the Bank of Japan," said Rhys Herbert, currency strategist at Prudential Portfolio Management.

Herbert sees little potential for appreciation against the dollar. "The key thing for us in terms of holding yen is that interest rates in Japan are so low that you have to be pretty optimistic to make it worthwhile."
Herbert thinks the Japanese economy will improve gradually in the next year, paving the way for a rise in interest rates.
"We are reasonably constructive on the Japanese equity market. We think it is more likely to do well in an environment where the yen is stable rather than rising."
Matthew Merritt, senior global strategist at ING Barings, sees relative stability in the yen at current levels before a greater period of dollar weakness in late 1997 and into 1998.
"As and when the economy picks up, (Japanese) interest rates are going to have to go higher," said Merritt.
He said Japanese authorities will continue to be wary about an appreciating yen after April's indirect tax rise.
"I find it difficult getting enthusiastic about Japan at these levels, I would have to underweight it in a global portfolio," Merritt said.
The Japanese consumer economy has done better than expected since April's tax rise, according to Heath.

He is moving towards a more balanced equity portfolio from a more export-oriented one. "If the economy is a bit stronger than expected that naturally leads one to be less slanted towards the exporting sectors. But 110-115 yen/dollar doesn't need to be negative for exporters. A level of 125 was a complete gift."

"The expectation was that the economy would grind to a halt following the tax rise and that hasn't happened. Compared to expectations of three months ago the situation is marginally better," Heath said.
